bib.title: Salesforce Koa: An Enterprise Language Model for Agentic Tool Use

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Salesforce Koa: An Enterprise Language Model for Agentic Tool Use", Zixiang Chen*, Sufeng Niu*, Yingchi Liu*, Wenting Zhao*, Akshara Prabhakar*, Shubham Mehrotra* (co-first) et al.; Salesforce Agentforce & AI Research; technical report (arXiv:2609.15066v2, cs.CL, 8 Oct 2026; PDF dated October 9, 2026). Preprint, no venue. First author: Zixiang Chen.
COVERAGE: 17 of 17 pages (53,919 chars), including appendices A-C. Nothing skipped. Figure 1 (p14) is a diagram and was not viewed as an image.

CLAIMS (ranked; note = bears on)
1. Koa (Nemotron-3-Super-120B + GRPO, FP8) gets 87% TSR on CRMAgentBench vs GPT-4.1 82%, base 79%, GPT-5.5 91%, Gemini 3.7 Flash 91%, Nemotron-Ultra-550B 87%. [notes 05, 07]
 setup: 97 tasks, 5 CRM domains, strict all-or-nothing, LLM user simulator. No seeds or CIs are reported. The Nemotron base is already RL-post-trained.
 quote: "It reaches 87% Task Success Rate on CRMAgentBench (vs. GPT-4.1 at 82% and the base at 79%)" (p1). Per-domain gains are Field Service 74→91 and Store Manager 76→86 (p6). Customer Service and Marketing are flat or lower than GPT-4.1 (Table 1).
2. Controlled ablation: adding an in-domain RL stage lifts human-labeled production tool-calling success from 0.825 to 0.842 (BF16) and 0.848 (FP8). [05, 06]
 setup: internal human-labeled set. Size not given. Recipe held fixed. Table 3 rows: base 0.819, +RL public 0.825, Koa BF16 0.842, FP8 0.848. Args 0.825→0.842→0.851.
 quote: "this in-domain stage improves success and argument accuracy from 0.825/0.825 to 0.842/0.842, and Salesforce Koa reaches 0.848/0.851." (p9)
 Total gain over base is about +3 points (0.819→0.848), single run. On the synthetic set, success is flat: 0.846 base, 0.845 RL, 0.845 BF16, 0.847 FP8.
3. Table 2 (human-labeled): Koa beats GPT-4.1 on all four metrics (Succ 0.848 vs 0.782). Its NoHall of 0.989 is the highest. On the synthetic multi-LLM-judged set, frontier models lead: GPT-5.5 0.902, GPT-4.1 0.897, Koa 0.847. Koa's synthetic Name score of 0.902 is below the base's 0.891 only marginally above, but below GPT-4.1 (0.937). [07]
 quote: "On the synthetic set the frontier models lead on success (GPT-5.5 0.902, GPT-4.1 0.897) while Koa scores 0.847." (p7)
 The reported model is "single-environment RL checkpoint (step 100) after FP8 post-training quantization".
4. Public RL stage 1 helps BFCL; the in-domain stage 2 gives some back. BFCL overall is base 64.73, +RL public 66.63, Koa BF16 64.31, FP8 63.87. Multi-turn is 54.12→59.50→57.50→53.50. [05, 06]
 quote: "the second in-domain stage costs 2.3 BFCL points (66.63→64.31) yet is the same stage that lifts the deployed task" (p10). Koa is at parity with base on BFCL, so "capability preserved" means no gain, not improvement.
5. SFT vs RL from an already post-trained base. Tau2 is SFT 70.04, RL 69.41, base 68.64. BFCL multi-turn is SFT 53.25 (down from 54.12) vs RL 59.50. CRM Bench is SFT 0.88 vs RL 0.86. [05]
 setup: SFT used synthetic APIGen/APIGen-MT data, 32 H200s, seq len 8192, batch 32, peak LR 5e-8 ("deliberately conservative"), full-parameter. The SFT recipe was not tuned beyond that, so the comparison is weak.
 quote: "SFT slightly reduces accuracy (54.12→53.25) whereas RL improves it substantially to 59.50" (p9).
6. Tau2Bench weighted average (GPT-4.1 simulator, 4 trials, pass^1): Koa 69.33, base 68.64, GPT-4.1 54.48, GPT-5.5 83.99. Telecom: Koa 59.2 vs GPT-5.5 95.8. [07]
7. FP8 PTQ (NVIDIA ModelOpt, in-domain calibration) keeps performance. Tau2 69.70→69.33, BFCL 64.31→63.87, CRM Bench 0.86→0.87. No latency, throughput or memory numbers are given. [10]
8. Reward design (Sec 3.2, App A.1). [06, 07]
 - Coverage reward: cov = resolved sub-questions / total, judged per numbered sub-question by a frozen Nano-30B helper. The same helper also plays customer simulator and tool emulator.
 - Duplicate-call gate: R = 0 if a consecutive duplicate tool call occurred.
 - Data-bound sub-questions count as resolved only if grounded in a successful tool call.
 - The deterministic sandbox uses binary state-equivalence reward.
 - Constrained-decision-turn mode: a needed tool is withheld, and the reward has a procedural gate plus a consequence score (App B.2).
9. GRPO variant (App B.1). [05, 10]
 - Leave-one-out group baseline with std normalization, clipped at c.
 - Dynamic sampling drops zero-variance groups.
 - One update per rollout batch, ratio forced to 1, no reference-KL, no clipped-ratio term.
 - Token-level truncated importance sampling (TIS) weight corrects the train/generation mismatch.
 - Malformed tool-call or thinking syntax gets a fixed negative advantage. Over-length or logprob-inconsistent trajectories are masked.
10. Spec-driven environments (Sec 3.1, 3.4). Agent Script specs compile to a typed workflow graph and are expanded into persona/scenario sessions executed in NeMo Gym. Public domains use synthesized structure: salesforce support, healthcare admin, real estate, and a helper-free workplace sandbox. The in-domain data is production Salesforce specs, but "only specification-derived and synthesized interactions". [06, 10]
11. Training infrastructure and cost (Sec 4.1, App B.3). [10]
 - 5 x B200 nodes: 4 actor nodes (32 B200s, colocated rollout and training) plus 1 helper node (8 B200s, TP=8).
 - Policy sharding TP=8, EP=8, PP=1 with sequence parallelism.
 - The helper is a single engine to avoid "a data-parallel coordination failure mode observed when the helper was split across replicas".
 - A Nano v3 (~30B) model was a cheap proxy for developing the recipe.
 - Serving is vLLM, 256K context.
 - COST: no GPU-hours, steps, dollars or batch/group sizes are reported (group size is only "small"). Only "step 100" is stated.
 - Training was "in partnership with NVIDIA".

LIMITS
- Authors concede: the base is already RL-post-trained, so "the preference for RL over SFT may not hold from a pre-RL checkpoint". Also "some enterprise evaluations use modest task counts" (p10).
- Not shown: seeds, variance or CIs; the human-labeled set size; judge-model identity for the synthetic split and for the LLM argument judge; training curves; reward-hacking analysis; ablation of the duplicate gate or coverage reward; helper size effect.
- The in-domain data and the production benchmark come from the same Salesforce distribution, and the paper does not describe any overlap check. All the headline gains are single-run with small differences (1-3 points).
- The internal benchmarks (production, CRM Bench) are not public and cannot be reproduced. GPT-4.1 BFCL numbers are from the public leaderboard, not a same-harness run (p8).
- The model-name and version strings (GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.7 Flash) are as printed.

BUILDS ON: GRPO (Shao 2024; DeepSeek-R1, Guo 2025); NeMo Gym (NVIDIA 2025-26); APIGen (Liu 2024) and APIGen-MT (Prabhakar 2025) for SFT data; Critical-State RL (Chen 2026, arXiv:2609.24985) for the constrained decision turns; PivotRL (Yi 2026); xLAM; Tau2-Bench (Barres 2025); BFCL (Patil 2025); CRMArena (Huang 2025); Agent Script (Salesforce 2026).

CODE: Eq. 2, p4: R = 0 if a consecutive duplicate tool call occurred, else cov. Eq. 3, p15: the GRPO loss with truncated IS weight w = min(τ, exp[log π_train − log π_gen]).

FIGURES: Fig. 1 (p14), one training rollout. It shows the trained policy against the frozen helper (simulator, emulator, judge), and the scalar reward emitted at the end by the coverage judge. Useful for note 06.

PROBLEMS: no embedded instructions found. Table text extraction lost bolding, so "best in column" is not visible. Some table rows were garbled (Table 1 GPT-4.1 columns). The GPT-4.1 Marketing/SDR values 90/95 and its Store Manager/Customer Service/Field Service values 67/77/83 are my best reading and are unverified.
